# About this document {#sec-about .unnumbered}

Amazon Web Services (AWS) rents out computers, storage, and hundreds of other
services by the second or the gigabyte. Everything in it is a resource, such
as a machine, a disk, or a bucket of files: it lives in one region of one
account, only those whom a permission names may use it, and it costs money for
as long as it exists, whether it is used or not. Almost every surprise on AWS,
above all the bill, follows from that (@sec-model). Working with it, for most
research software, comes down to logging in, keeping data in S3, and renting
machines on EC2 (@sec-usage).

Every action in the web console is a call to the same interface that the
command-line tool `aws` and the libraries, such as boto3 in Python, call. What
can be clicked can be scripted, and a script records what was done, which
clicks do not ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-recipe)). This document uses
the command-line tool. Beyond S3 and EC2, AWS Batch runs many jobs in
containers from a queue, much like Slurm ([](../scheduling/slurm.qmd)), and
ParallelCluster sets up a cluster with Slurm on AWS.

Checked against the AWS CLI 2.38.


# How AWS thinks {#sec-model}

An account holds resources and receives their bill; organizations often give
each project an account of its own. A region is a group of data centers, such
as `eu-central-1` in Frankfurt, and almost every resource lives in exactly
one. Permissions, in Identity and Access Management (IAM), say who may do what
with which resource; whatever no permission allows is denied.


## Everything costs for as long as it exists {#sec-costs}

AWS bills resources while they exist, not while they are used. A machine bills
while it runs, its disk as long as the disk exists, even when the machine is
stopped, and data in S3 every month. The usual surprise on the bill is a
forgotten resource: a machine with a GPU left running over a holiday, the
disks of machines stopped long ago, or a bucket of intermediate files. Set a
budget with an alert in the console, under Billing, before anything else; tag
every resource with its project, such as `project=ocean`; and end what is no
longer needed, in every region that was used, because the console shows most
resources one region at a time.

Moving data costs as well. Uploading data into AWS is free, and so is moving
it between S3 and machines in the same region, but downloading it out of AWS,
or between regions, is charged per gigabyte. Keep the computation in the region
of the data, and bring back only results, not raw data.


## Nothing is allowed unless granted {#sec-iam}

Every call to AWS carries credentials, and IAM checks them against
permissions. People log in through the single sign-on of their organization,
IAM Identity Center, and get credentials that expire after some hours
(@sec-login). Programs on a machine in AWS get theirs from a role attached to
the machine, without any keys. Keys that never expire, an access key ID and a
secret, are the last resort: never write them into code, a notebook, or a
repository, where they are found and used within hours of a push. Grant a
person or a program only what it needs, such as reading one bucket.

A region is also a jurisdiction: data stay in the region they were put in,
which matters for personal data, such as patient records under the GDPR.


## S3: objects, not files {#sec-s3}

S3 stores objects in buckets. An object is a key, such as
`data/raw/s1.csv`, and its bytes, written whole and replaced whole: in an
ordinary bucket, there is no appending to an object and no changing part of
it. There are no
directories, only keys that share a beginning, a prefix, which the tools show
as directories. Renaming a "directory" copies and deletes every object under
its prefix. Bucket names are global across all accounts, so a name such as
`data` is long taken; name buckets after the organization and the project.

Formats that read only the parts they need, by requests for ranges of bytes or
for single objects, work well from S3, such as Parquet
([](../data/parquet.qmd#sec-columns)) and Zarr, which writes one object per
chunk ([](../data/zarr.qmd#sec-chunks)). Versioning, switched on per bucket,
keeps the old versions of overwritten and deleted objects, a cheap protection
against a script that writes to the wrong prefix.


## EC2: machines by the second {#sec-ec2}

An EC2 instance is a virtual machine. Its instance type fixes the CPUs, the
memory, and the GPUs, such as `c7i.4xlarge` with 16 CPUs and 32 GB, and its
image, an AMI, the operating system it starts from. Its disk is an EBS volume,
which survives when the instance is stopped and, by default, is deleted when it
is terminated. Some types also have fast local disks, which lose their data
when the instance stops. Stopping an instance ends the bill for the machine but
not for its disk; terminating it ends both, and deletes its disk.

Spot instances run on capacity that AWS has spare, for a fraction of the
price, but AWS can take them back at two minutes' notice. They suit work that
saves checkpoints and can resume ([](../scheduling/slurm.qmd#sec-checkpoint)).
New accounts may start only few CPUs, and often no GPUs at all; ask for higher
quotas, under Service Quotas, days before they are needed.


# Working with AWS {#sec-usage}

The examples assume a profile `lab` and a bucket `lab-ocean-data` in
`eu-central-1`. Every command takes `--region` and `--profile`, which
otherwise come from the profile or the variables `AWS_REGION` and
`AWS_PROFILE`.


## Log in {#sec-login}

```bash
aws configure sso                 # once: the portal of the organization
aws sso login --profile lab       # every day: credentials for some hours
export AWS_PROFILE=lab
aws sts get-caller-identity       # who am I, and in which account
```

`aws configure sso` asks for the address of the portal of the organization and
saves a profile in `~/.aws/config`. The libraries that read from AWS, such as
boto3, Polars, and s3fs, find the credentials of the profile themselves, so
code does not handle them. `aws sts get-caller-identity` shows which account
the commands that follow act on, before anything is created or deleted.


## Keep data in S3 {#sec-s3-usage}

```bash
aws s3 mb s3://lab-ocean-data --region eu-central-1
aws s3 cp results/fit.json s3://lab-ocean-data/results/fit.json
aws s3 sync data/ s3://lab-ocean-data/data/
aws s3 sync data/ s3://lab-ocean-data/data/ --delete --dryrun
aws s3 ls s3://lab-ocean-data/data/ --recursive --human-readable --summarize
aws s3 presign s3://lab-ocean-data/results/fit.json --expires-in 86400
```

`sync` copies only what is missing or has changed, in either direction, and
with `--delete` also deletes what the source no longer has: check that with
`--dryrun` first. `presign` prints an address by which anyone can download one
object, here for a day, without an account. Code reads from S3 by address:

```python
import polars as pl
import xarray as xr

samples = pl.read_parquet("s3://lab-ocean-data/data/samples.parquet")
ocean = xr.open_zarr("s3://lab-ocean-data/ocean.zarr")    # needs s3fs
```


## Run a machine on EC2 {#sec-ec2-usage}

```bash
aws ec2 run-instances --image-id ami-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --instance-type c7i.4xlarge --key-name lab --tag-specifications \
    'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=project,Value=ocean}]'
aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=instance-state-name,Values=running \
    --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].[InstanceId,InstanceType,LaunchTime]' \
    --output table
aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids i-0abc123def4567890
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids i-0abc123def4567890
```

The ID of the image depends on the region; the console lists the current
images of Ubuntu, Amazon Linux, and others, and the Deep Learning AMIs come
with the drivers of the GPUs and CUDA. `--key-name` names an SSH key that was
created or imported in the region, by which `ssh -i lab.pem ubuntu@<address>`
logs in, with `ec2-user` instead of `ubuntu` on Amazon Linux. A security group,
the firewall of the instance, has to allow SSH, and only from the address of
the person who logs in.

Record the instance type, the ID of the image, and the region with the results
they produced, together with the image of the container the code ran in
([](../containers/index.qmd#sec-record)). Copy results to S3 before
terminating an instance: its disk goes with it.
